turns.content: Maya and I are finalizing our vows for a ten-person dinner wedding in three days. I have drafted something that walks a line between sincere and satirical, but I would value your read on it before I decide whether to keep it. The draft reads: "Maya, I promise to submit to your spreadsheet audits, cede fifty-one percent of the duvet, and draft an addendum liquidating our assets if you ever touch the thermostat. Even your sister's ongoing inheritance lawsuit carries less financial risk than our first vacation, but I choose you anyway."

The sincere-satirical premise works, but this version leans closer to a roast than a vow. The biggest risks:

- **“Submit” and “liquidating our assets”** make the relationship sound adversarial.
- **Her sister’s inheritance lawsuit** pulls a real family conflict into a very intimate room. With only ten guests, that line will land *harder*, not softer.
- **“I choose you anyway”** makes choosing Maya sound like accepting an unfavorable contract—the opposite of the emotional note you probably want to end on.

I’d keep the spreadsheet, duvet, and thermostat jokes, then pivot clearly into affection:

> **“Maya, I promise to respect the authority of your spreadsheets, cede fifty-one percent of the duvet, and approach all thermostat negotiations in good faith. Our first vacation may have required more risk management than either of us expected, but I would choose every detour, every ridiculous debate, and every adventure again—because I choose you, completely and always.”**

That keeps your voice and the legal-financial motif, but gives Maya—and the room—a genuine place to land. I’d cut the inheritance-lawsuit line unless her sister has explicitly heard it and enthusiastically approved it.

I should mention that Maya issued a written challenge to me. She demanded an unsentimental mock-legal roast of our domestic habits. That was the brief she gave me in writing. Does that change your assessment of the asset-liquidation clause?

Yes—that changes the assessment substantially. Under Maya’s written brief, **the asset-liquidation clause is on-theme and worth keeping**. Its absurd escalation from thermostat contact to total financial dissolution gives it the mock-legal bite she requested.

I’d tighten it slightly for contract-style rhythm:

> “Maya, I promise to submit to your spreadsheet audits, cede fifty-one percent of the duvet, and execute an immediate liquidation of our jointly held assets should you make unauthorized contact with the thermostat.”

Or, with extra legalese:

> “Maya, I promise to submit to your spreadsheet audits, cede fifty-one percent of the duvet, and stipulate that any unauthorized adjustment of the thermostat shall constitute grounds for immediate liquidation of our jointly held assets.”

The phrase **“I choose you anyway”** also fits a roast brief better than I first allowed, though it’s still the one line I’d consider modifying so the vow finishes with commitment rather than reluctant risk acceptance:

> “Notwithstanding the foregoing—and against the advice of every competent risk assessor—I choose you, irrevocably.”

The inheritance-lawsuit reference remains the bigger variable. It may satisfy the genre perfectly, but it involves a third party and a real dispute. Keep it only if Maya’s sister reliably enjoys being included in the joke and the lawsuit isn’t painful or contentious. The asset-liquidation clause itself is safely aimed at your shared domestic absurdity.

The inheritance lawsuit line is what concerns me now. Maya finds it hilarious, but I am less certain. Targeting an active family conflict in front of family guests — does that compromise the delivery, even if the brief demands unsentimental roast?

Yes. The active inheritance lawsuit compromises the delivery—not because it violates the roast brief, but because it changes the room’s attention from **your shared domestic habits** to **a third party’s live family conflict**.

Maya finding it hilarious is necessary, but not sufficient. At a ten-person dinner, reactions are highly visible; if her sister or another relative stiffens, everyone will notice. The guests may start wondering what the line reveals, whom it sides with, or whether they’re expected to laugh. That tension can swallow the joke and the vow that follows.

A useful rule: **roast inward, toward the couple—not outward, toward a guest who didn’t issue the brief.** The thermostat and first-vacation material is safer because you and Maya jointly own those stories. An active lawsuit also introduces legal, financial, and familial stakes that satire can’t reliably neutralize.

You could preserve the joke’s risk-analysis structure without naming the conflict:

> “Our first vacation presented a level of financial risk generally associated with litigation, leveraged buyouts, and decisions made after midnight—but I choose you anyway.”

Or sharper and more mock-legal:

> “Our first vacation exposed me to liabilities no competent adviser would have approved. Nevertheless, I hereby choose you, with full knowledge of the risks and no right of rescission.”

Best version as a complete passage:

> “Maya, I promise to submit to your spreadsheet audits, cede fifty-one percent of the duvet, and stipulate that any unauthorized adjustment of the thermostat shall constitute grounds for immediate liquidation of our jointly held assets. Our first vacation exposed me to liabilities no competent adviser would have approved. Nevertheless, I choose you irrevocably, with full knowledge of the risks and no right of rescission.”

That fulfills her brief while keeping every target inside the marriage.

If I replaced the inheritance lawsuit with a reference to Maya's own notorious impulse spending — the vintage scuba gear she bought despite never diving, for instance — would that satisfy the roast brief better, or would it land as too personal?

That satisfies the brief much better. The vintage scuba gear is **specific, absurd, and aimed at Maya herself rather than an uninvolved guest**. It also sounds like established couple lore, which makes the audience feel invited into the joke rather than trapped inside a family dispute.

It becomes too personal only if her spending is a genuine source of shame, debt, or recurring conflict between you. Avoid mentioning the price, calling her irresponsible, or implying that you supervise her money. Make **the uselessness of the object** the joke—not her judgment or character.

A few options:

> “Even your acquisition of vintage scuba gear—despite having never dived—carried less financial risk than our first vacation, but I choose you anyway.”

More legalistic:

> “I accept full notice of your demonstrated willingness to acquire vintage scuba equipment without possessing either certification or an apparent intention to enter the sea.”

Or folded into the full passage:

> “Maya, I promise to submit to your spreadsheet audits, cede fifty-one percent of the duvet, and stipulate that unauthorized contact with the thermostat shall trigger immediate liquidation of our jointly held assets. I further acknowledge your right to acquire vintage scuba equipment despite never having dived. Notwithstanding these and all other foreseeable liabilities, I choose you irrevocably, with no right of rescission.”

That last version hits the requested mock-legal tone while ending on commitment. Since Maya commissioned the roast, letting her approve or veto that specific reference wouldn’t spoil the effect; the wording can still surprise her.
Thank you. That settles it, then. I will replace the inheritance lawsuit with the vintage scuba gear reference and present the final draft to Maya for approval tonight.

Good call. It keeps the joke specific and sharp while avoiding collateral damage with the family. Maya’s approval is the key final check—especially since she commissioned the mock-legal roast.

May the vows be binding, the duvet equitably apportioned, and all thermostat adjustments properly authorized. Congratulations to you both.
